source_first_audit.profile_reason: Previous bounded draft exceeded pre-draft budget by about two minutes; preserve validated draft and complete source-first.

facts.statement: American pronunciation has primary stress on the first syllable and permits final /tuːt/ or /tjuːt/.
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster headword pronunciation line records /ˈkän(t)-stə-ˌtüt/ and /-ˌtyüt/.

facts.statement: Constituted is the past tense and past participle; constituting is the present participle.
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster inflection line lists constituted and constituting and labels constitute transitive.

facts.statement: Parts or members constitute a whole by making it up, forming it, or composing it.
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster sense 1 defines constitute as make up, form, compose and gives twelve months constitute a year.

facts.statement: Constitute can mean to set up, establish, or found an institution or government.
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster sense 2 includes set up, establish, and constitute a provisional government.

facts.statement: In legal use constitute can give an agreement or body due or lawful form.
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster general and legal definitions record giving due or required legal form.

facts.statement: Constitute can appoint a person to an office, function, or dignity.
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster sense 3 and legal sense 1 explicitly record appointment to an office or function.

facts.statement: An act or document may constitute something by qualifying as it, as when failure to act constitutes negligence.
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster legal sense 3b defines qualify as and illustrates failure to act may constitute negligence.

facts.statement: Constitute came through Middle English from Latin constitutus, the participle of constituere, from com- plus statuere to set.
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster Word History gives the Middle English and Latin derivation and links statuere with set.

facts.statement: British pronunciation uses /ɒ/ and /tjuːt/, while the American form commonly uses /tuːt/.
facts.source_detail: Collins COBUILD and British/American pronunciation entries contrast UK /ˈkɒnstɪtjuːt/ with a US ending /tuːt/.

facts.statement: The equivalence sense is a non-continuous linking-like verb followed directly by a noun phrase.
facts.source_detail: Collins COBUILD labels the sense link verb, no continuous, with the pattern VERB noun and examples constitute an offence and constitute a victory.

facts.statement: People or things constitute a whole when they are the parts or members forming it, including a stated percentage.
facts.source_detail: Collins COBUILD sense 2 defines the parts-to-whole relation and illustrates volunteers constituting over 95 percent of a workforce.

facts.statement: A committee, government, court, or similar body is constituted when formally established and authorized to operate.
facts.source_detail: Collins COBUILD sense 3 and British senses 3-4 record formal establishment and legal form for institutions and courts.

facts.statement: Constitute can give a person an office or function, including in passive constituted expressions.
facts.source_detail: Collins British and American entries define appointment and give legally constituted officer and he was constituted treasurer.

facts.statement: The passive construction constituted of can identify the materials or parts composing a whole.
facts.source_detail: Collins American entry illustrates mortar constituted of lime and sand.

facts.statement: The physical sense set or place is archaic.
facts.source_detail: Collins American sense 6 explicitly labels to set or place archaic.

facts.statement: The formal-establishment use is formal and is commonly realized in the passive.
facts.source_detail: Collins COBUILD labels the body-establishment sense formal and usually passive.

facts.statement: The parts-to-whole formation sense is recorded from the mid-fifteenth century.
facts.source_detail: Etymonline dates the formation-as-a-necessary-part sense to the mid-15th century.

facts.statement: Latin constituere covered causing to stand, setting up, fixing, establishing, and forming something new.
facts.source_detail: Etymonline lists these meanings for Latin constituere.

facts.statement: The appoint-to-office sense is historically old and is recorded from around 1400.
facts.source_detail: Etymonline dates appoint or elect to an office or position of power to about 1400.

facts.statement: The Latin source combines an assimilated form of com- with statuere to set, ultimately related to the root meaning stand.
facts.source_detail: Etymonline analyzes constituere as com- plus statuere and connects statuere to the PIE root meaning stand.

facts.statement: Constitution is a noun for structure or physical makeup and for fundamental governing principles or their written instrument.
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster constitution senses cover physical makeup, structure, organization, fundamental laws, and the written governing instrument.

facts.statement: Constitutional is an adjective for constitution-related, constitution-authorized, bodily-constitution, or fundamental-makeup senses.
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster adjective senses cover constitutional law, bodily makeup, and fundamental makeup.

facts.statement: Constitutionally is the adverb derived from constitutional.
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster records constitutionally as an adverb under constitutional.

facts.statement: Constituent as a noun can mean an essential component or a member of a political constituency.
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster noun senses distinguish component and constituency-member meanings.

facts.statement: Constituent as an adjective means serving to form or make up a whole.
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster adjective sense 1 defines constituent as forming or composing a whole.

facts.statement: Reconstitute means constitute again or anew, especially restore by adding water or another liquid.
facts.source_detail: Merriam-Webster defines reconstitute as constitute again or anew and especially restore by adding water.

source_union.canonical_statement: Constitute has first-syllable primary stress, with UK /ɒ/ and /tjuːt/ and common US /ɑː/ and /tuːt/ realizations.
source_union.rationale: The pronunciation section records the regionally differentiated forms.

source_union.canonical_statement: Constituted and constituting are the principal inflected forms of the transitive verb constitute.
source_union.rationale: Inflections and their pronunciation are taught explicitly.

source_union.canonical_statement: Parts, members, or a category constitute a whole or a share of it in the parts-to-whole sense.
source_union.rationale: Sense 1 and its central frames directly express this well-attested relation.

source_union.canonical_statement: An act, fact, or situation constitutes a category when it qualifies as or can be regarded as that category.
source_union.rationale: Sense 2 separates this linking-like classification meaning from composition.

source_union.canonical_statement: Constitute formally establishes and authorizes an institution, committee, government, court, or similar body.
source_union.rationale: Sense 3 covers formal institutional establishment and its passive realization.

source_union.canonical_statement: In formal or legal language constitute can appoint a person to an office or function.
source_union.rationale: Sense 4 includes both direct-complement and as-complement appointment frames and labels their register.

source_union.canonical_statement: Constitute can give a body or agreement the form required for legal validity.
source_union.rationale: The lawful-form aspect is integrated into the formal-establishment sense without asserting universal legal effects.

source_union.canonical_statement: The passive constituted of construction may identify the components of a whole.
source_union.rationale: Sense 1 teaches this formal passive alongside the active direction contrast.

source_union.canonical_statement: Constitute derives through Middle English from Latin constituere, built from com- and statuere and associated with setting or establishing.
source_union.rationale: The etymology section presents the attested source and a restrained semantic bridge.

source_union.canonical_statement: Constitution is the related noun for makeup or structure and for fundamental governing principles or their document.
source_union.rationale: The word-formation section records these principal learner-relevant senses.

source_union.canonical_statement: Constitutional is the related adjective for bodily or structural makeup and for a governing constitution.
source_union.rationale: The word-formation section records both broad sense families.

source_union.canonical_statement: Constitutionally is the adverb derived from constitutional.
source_union.rationale: The word-formation section identifies the adverb and its broad meanings.

source_union.canonical_statement: Constituent is a related noun for a component or constituency member and an adjective meaning forming a whole.
source_union.rationale: The word-formation section distinguishes the noun and adjective and warns against confusing the political noun with a verb object.

source_union.canonical_statement: Reconstitute means constitute anew or restore a material by adding liquid.
source_union.rationale: The word-formation section records both the compositional and specialized restoration meanings.

source_union.canonical_statement: The physical set-or-place sense of constitute is archaic.
source_union.rationale: The generation inventory excludes this obsolete physical-placement sense because it has negligible modern learner value.

claim_units.statement: Constitute has regionally differentiated UK and US pronunciation patterns.

source_supports.support_summary: Merriam-Webster directly records the American stressed form and /tuːt/ or /tjuːt/ variation.
Collins independently contrasts British /ɒ, tjuːt/ with the common American /tuːt/ ending.

claim_units.statement: Constituted and constituting are regular inflected forms of constitute.

source_supports.support_summary: Merriam-Webster explicitly lists constituted and constituting as the verb's inflected forms.

claim_units.statement: Parts or members constitute a whole, and a category may constitute a stated share of the whole.

source_supports.support_summary: Merriam-Webster defines the parts-to-whole sense as make up, form, or compose.
Collins independently defines members forming a whole and supplies a percentage example.
Etymonline confirms that the formation-as-a-part meaning is historically established.

claim_units.statement: A fact or act constitutes a category when it qualifies as or can be regarded as that category.

source_supports.support_summary: Merriam-Webster legal usage directly defines constitute as qualify as and illustrates negligence.
Collins independently defines the regarded-as sense and specifies the direct VERB-noun pattern.

claim_units.statement: Constitute can formally establish and authorize an institution or public body.

source_supports.support_summary: Merriam-Webster directly records set up, establish, found, and provisional-government use.
Collins independently defines formal establishment and authorization for committees and governments.
Collins marks this institutional-establishment sense formal and commonly passive.
Etymonline supplies the Latin establish-and-form semantic history supporting the restrained bridge.

claim_units.statement: Formal or legal constitute can appoint a person to an office or role.

source_supports.support_summary: Merriam-Webster directly defines appointment to an office, function, or dignity.
Collins independently records legally constituted officer and constituted treasurer.
Etymonline records the appointment sense as an old use, supporting the register warning.

claim_units.statement: Constitute may give a body or agreement the required official or lawful form.

source_supports.support_summary: Merriam-Webster explicitly records giving an agreement or body due or required legal form.

claim_units.statement: Constituted of may present the whole first and its component materials after of.

source_supports.support_summary: Collins directly illustrates the passive constituted of construction with material components.

claim_units.statement: Constitute descends through Middle English from Latin constituere, involving com- and statuere.

source_supports.support_summary: Merriam-Webster gives the Middle English and Latin participial derivation.
Etymonline independently analyzes the com- plus statuere formation and stand root.

claim_units.statement: Constitution is the related noun for makeup, structure, or fundamental governing principles.

source_supports.support_summary: Merriam-Webster directly records structure, physical makeup, governing principles, and document senses.

claim_units.statement: Constitutional is the related adjective for bodily or structural makeup and governing-constitution senses.

source_supports.support_summary: Merriam-Webster directly records constitutional adjective senses for makeup and a governing constitution.

claim_units.statement: Constitutionally is the adverb derived from constitutional.

source_supports.support_summary: Merriam-Webster explicitly lists constitutionally as the corresponding adverb.

claim_units.statement: Constituent can be a component or constituency member noun and a whole-forming adjective.

source_supports.support_summary: Merriam-Webster distinguishes the component and political constituency-member noun senses.
Merriam-Webster separately defines the adjective as serving to form or compose a whole.

claim_units.statement: Reconstitute means constitute anew and can mean restore by adding liquid.

source_supports.support_summary: Merriam-Webster directly defines both constitute anew and restoration by adding water.
